papers.title: PRKCD Orchestrates Sevoflurane-Induced Cognitive Dysfunction in Aged Rats by Regulating PINK1/PRKN Mitophagy Pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the protein PRKCD influences cognitive impairment caused by sevoflurane anesthesia in aged rats. The researchers found that PRKCD regulates mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) through the PINK1/PRKN signaling pathway. Their findings suggest that targeting this pathway could help prevent or treat anesthesia-related cognitive decline in elderly subjects.
papers.why: This paper directly examines PINK1/PRKN-mediated mitophagy in the aging brain, a core mechanistic pathway relevant to understanding mitophagy dysfunction in neurons.

papers.title: Activation of pro-survival autophagy by a small molecule promoting p62 oligomerisation.
papers.summary: This paper describes a small molecule that promotes autophagy, a cellular recycling process, by encouraging the protein p62 to cluster together into oligomers. This clustering activity appears to boost autophagy in a way that supports cell survival rather than triggering cell death. The work likely characterizes the molecule's mechanism and its effects on autophagic flux in cellular models.
papers.why: Since p62 is a key autophagy receptor and mitophagy regulator, a compound that boosts pro-survival autophagy could serve as a valuable pharmacological tool to modulate mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurons for studying their role in interneuron health and perineuronal net maintenance.

papers.title: p62/SQSTM1: From an autophagy receptor to a condensate organizer of selective autophagy and stress signaling.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how the protein p62/SQSTM1 has evolved conceptually from being seen as just a cargo receptor for selective autophagy into being recognized as a key organizer of biomolecular condensates. These condensates form through phase separation and help concentrate ubiquitinated proteins, damaged organelles, and stress signaling components together for efficient clearance. The review likely discusses how p62 condensates link autophagy machinery to cellular stress responses like the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and NF-kB signaling.
papers.why: Since p62/SQSTM1 is a central hub linking selective autophagy (including mitophagy) to cellular stress and protein aggregation, understanding its condensate-forming role could inform how neurons, especially interneurons, manage organelle quality control and proteostasis in ways that may be visualized or quantified using spatial omics and imaging approaches.

papers.summary: This paper appears to focus on the relationship between TBK1, a kinase, and IRGQ, a protein involved in autophagy regulation. papers.title: Dual Regulation of ACSL3 by TRIM33-Mediated Ubiquitination and NBR1-Dependent Autophagy: A Therapeutic Target for Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury.
papers.summary: This study looks at how a protein called ACSL3, which is involved in lipid metabolism, gets controlled by two different processes in the brain during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (a stroke-like event where blood flow is cut off then restored). One process involves TRIM33 tagging ACSL3 with ubiquitin, a molecular label that often marks proteins for degradation. The other involves NBR1, a receptor protein that helps direct tagged proteins into the autophagy pathway (the cell's recycling system) for breakdown, and together these regulate ACSL3 levels with potential therapeutic implications for stroke.
papers.why: While focused on ischemia rather than neurodegeneration or interneuron biology specifically, this paper offers relevant mechanistic insight into selective autophagy receptor (NBR1) and ubiquitin-mediated regulation of a metabolic enzyme in neurons, which could inform understanding of mitophagy/autophagy crosstalk with lipid metabolism in brain tissue.

papers.title: CCDC50 Alleviates Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury via Enhancing Autophagy to Inhibit STING/IRF3-Mediated Microglial Polarization.
papers.summary: This study looks at CCDC50, a protein that appears to protect the brain from damage caused by cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (like what happens after a stroke). The researchers found that CCDC50 works by boosting autophagy, the cell's internal recycling and cleanup process. This enhanced autophagy in turn suppresses a signaling pathway called STING/IRF3, which reduces harmful inflammatory activation (polarization) of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells.
papers.why: While this paper centers on microglia rather than neurons directly, its detailed mechanistic dissection of autophagy regulating neuroinflammatory signaling in the brain offers useful comparative insight for understanding autophagy/mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal health and interneuron vulnerability in ischemic or stressed brain tissue.

papers.title: Defective ferritinophagy was involved in high glucose-induced neuron oxidative damage in ND7/23 cells.
papers.summary: This study examines how high glucose levels affect neurons in the ND7/23 cell line, focusing on ferritinophagy, a selective autophagy process that degrades ferritin to release iron. The researchers found that ferritinophagy becomes defective under high glucose conditions, leading to disrupted iron regulation and increased oxidative damage in the neurons. This suggests that impaired ferritinophagy may be a mechanism contributing to neuronal damage seen in diabetic conditions.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it explores a specific autophagy pathway (ferritinophagy) linked to neuronal oxidative stress, offering mechanistic insight that complements broader mitophagy/autophagy research in neurons even though it doesn't directly address interneurons or perineuronal nets.

papers.title: The gut-brain-mitophagy axis: Urolithin A as a transcriptional activator of Parkin in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
papers.summary: This paper discusses Urolithin A, a gut-derived metabolite, as a molecule that can activate Parkin, a key protein involved in mitophagy (the process of clearing damaged mitochondria). It explores how this compound may influence neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's by boosting mitochondrial quality control in the brain. The work frames this within a 'gut-brain-mitophagy axis,' suggesting gut-derived signals can transcriptionally regulate mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal health.
papers.why: Understanding transcriptional activators of Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neurodegenerative disease contexts directly informs mechanistic models relevant to studying mitophagy dysfunction in neurons and interneurons within the brain.
